# Cardiac Contractility Modulation Therapy for Heart Failure: A Narrative Review

## Introduction

Despite major pharmacological and device-based advances, heart failure (HF) remains a leading cause of morbidity and mortality, and a substantial proportion of patients remain symptomatic on optimal medical therapy [1]. Cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT) benefits patients with a wide QRS complex, but roughly two-thirds of HF patients have a normal or only mildly prolonged QRS duration and are therefore not candidates [2]. Cardiac contractility modulation (CCM) was developed to address this therapeutic gap. CCM is an electrical device-based therapy for chronic heart failure that delivers nonexcitatory electrical signals applied during the cardiac absolute refractory period; these signals have myocardial effects including phosphorylation of key proteins involved with calcium cycling and shifts of myocardial gene expression from a fetal genotype typical of chronic heart failure toward a more normal adult genotype [3].

## Mechanisms of Action

CCM signals are delivered to the right ventricular septum during the absolute refractory period, so that they augment contraction without triggering a new action potential [4]. These high-amplitude, biphasic impulses appear to alter intracellular calcium handling, resulting in an increase in myocardial contractility without an associated increase in oxygen consumption [5]. The acute inotropic effect is striking: within one beat of initiating the CCM signal, contractility in isolated rabbit papillary muscle strips increases, and in cardiac trabeculae from patients with severe heart failure CCM raises baseline contractility by over 50% [6]. That this occurs without increased energetic cost was demonstrated when acute studies in dogs with experimentally induced heart failure showed that CCM signals applied to the failing myocardium during the absolute refractory period improved left ventricular function without increasing myocardial oxygen consumption [7].

Beyond acute effects, CCM induces favorable molecular and structural remodeling. At the cellular level CCM improves calcium handling through phosphorylation of phospholamban and upregulation of SERCA-2A, with reversal of the fetal myocyte gene program [8]. In a canine HF model, long-term delivery of CCM electric signals improved left ventricular function and global, cellular, and molecular remodeling [7]. These effects are initially evident in the region near the stimulation electrodes and, over weeks to months, become evident in regions remote from the stimulation site [3]. Comprehensive mechanistic synthesis confirms that CCM has been shown in HFrEF patients to improve calcium handling, to reverse the fetal myocyte gene programme associated with HF, and to facilitate reverse remodelling [9].

## Clinical Evidence

Early randomized data came from the FIX-HF-4 study. This randomized, double-blind, crossover study enrolled 164 subjects with ejection fraction below 35% and NYHA class II or III symptoms who received a CCM pulse generator [10]. The pivotal FIX-HF-5 trial followed. CCM was tested in 428 NYHA class III or IV, narrow-QRS heart failure patients with ejection fraction ≤35% randomized to optimal medical therapy plus CCM versus optimal medical therapy alone, with efficacy assessed by ventilatory anaerobic threshold and peak VO2 and a noninferiority safety endpoint of the composite of all-cause mortality and hospitalizations [11]. The study met its primary safety endpoint but did not reach its primary efficacy endpoint; however, in a prespecified subgroup analysis, significant improvements in primary and secondary endpoints were observed in patients with ejection fractions between 25% and 45% [12,13].

This signal prompted the confirmatory FIX-HF-5C trial. A total of 160 patients with NYHA class III or IV symptoms, QRS below 130 ms, and ejection fraction 25–45% were randomized to control or CCM; the difference in peak VO2 between groups was 0.84 mL O2/kg/min, satisfying the primary endpoint [14]. CCM was subsequently delivered by a simplified system: prior studies used a 3-lead Optimizer system, and a new 2-lead system eliminated the need for an atrial lead, evaluated in the FIX-HF-5C2 study [15].

A pooled analysis strengthened these findings. In 2020, a comprehensive individual patient data meta-analysis of randomized trials plus the nonrandomized FIX-HF-5C2 included 861 patients, and showed that CCM significantly improved peak VO2, 6-minute walk test distance, and quality of life by the Minnesota Living with Heart Failure Questionnaire [16].

## Real-World and Long-Term Outcomes

Registry and observational data support durability of benefit. The CCM-REG registry reported that long-term CCM delivered by the Optimizer Smart system was assessed in a prospective registry including 503 patients from 51 European centres for effects on quality of life, ejection fraction, mortality, and hospitalizations [17], with reductions in HF hospitalization rates and improvements in NYHA class and ejection fraction [18]. A two-year multicenter evaluation found that CCM can improve symptoms in this population, with the first 2-year multi-site evaluation reporting outcomes in patients with HF and reduced ejection fraction [19]. Observational case-control work also suggested CCM may improve long-term survival relative to predicted estimates [20].

## Expanding Indications

CCM is being explored across the EF spectrum. A study of CCM signals demonstrated improved exercise intolerance and maladaptive regulation of cardiac key proteins for systolic and diastolic function in HFpEF [21], and the CCM-HFpEF pilot study assessed the potential benefits of CCM in patients with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction [22], with the AIM-HIGHer trial now testing this prospectively [23]. Mechanistic reasoning suggests CCM is particularly beneficial in patients with baseline EF between 35% and 45%, which includes half the range of patients with mid-range EF [9,24].

## Patient Selection and Guidelines

Current evidence supports CCM in patients who remain symptomatic despite guideline-directed medical treatment without an indication for CRT and have a left ventricular ejection fraction ranging from 25 to 45% [25]. Recent US FDA labeling specifically removed the requirement for normal sinus rhythm, allowing CCM in patients with HFrEF who are in atrial fibrillation [26]. CCM was first discussed in European HF guidelines in 2016 [27] and is referenced in the 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA HF guideline [28]. Importantly, CCM is generally well tolerated and is compatible with existing pharmacological therapies and does not interact negatively with implantable cardioverter-defibrillators or CRT devices [29], and is typically implanted with conscious sedation given that the leads can cause diaphragmatic stimulation [30].

## Conclusion

CCM has matured from a mechanistic curiosity into a clinically available therapy that improves exercise capacity, symptoms, and quality of life in symptomatic HFrEF and HFmrEF patients with narrow QRS who are not CRT candidates. Adequately powered randomized trials assessing hard outcomes—and the role of CCM in HFpEF—will further define its place in HF management.
